text: The provided passages do not answer this question. They only list specific examples of high-risk AI systems within the law enforcement and migration sectors but do not define the general term "AI system" under the Act.

A "serious incident" is defined as an incident or malfunctioning of an AI system that directly or indirectly leads to specific outcomes. These outcomes include the death of a person or serious harm to a person's health, a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure, the infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights, or serious harm to property or the environment [1].

A general-purpose AI model is an AI model, including where such a model is trained with a large amount of data using self-supervision at scale, that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of the way the model is placed on the market [1]. It must also be capable of being integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications, except for models used for research, development, or prototyping activities before they are placed on the market [1].

No, the deployer obligations do not apply to you because the Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity [1].

The rules do not cover research, testing, or development activities regarding AI systems prior to them being placed on the market or put into service, as these are excluded from the Regulation [1]. However, for high-risk AI systems, testing must be performed at any time throughout the development process and, in any event, prior to being placed on the market or put into service [2]. Additionally, providers may conduct testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions at any time before the placing on the market or the putting into service of the system [3].

The data governance practices must cover relevant design choices, data collection processes and origins, and data-preparation operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment, and aggregation [1]. These practices must also include the formulation of assumptions regarding what the data measures, an assessment of data availability and suitability, and an examination for biases affecting health, safety, fundamental rights, or discrimination [1]. Furthermore, the practices must involve measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate identified biases, as well as the identification of data gaps that prevent compliance with the Regulation [1]. The data sets themselves must be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors, and complete for the intended purpose [2]. Additionally, the data sets must take into account characteristics particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional setting of the system's use [5].

Yes, high-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system [3]. Providers of high-risk AI systems are required to keep these automatically generated logs to the extent they are under their control [1]. Similarly, deployers must keep the logs automatically generated by the system if they are under their control [2]. These logs must be retained for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law [1][2].

Yes, a provider established in a third country must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union prior to making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market [3]. This requirement applies before the system is placed on the market or put into service [2]. The importer must also verify that the provider has appointed such a representative in accordance with Article 22(1) [5].

Yes, a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data, such as ethnicity, to detect and correct bias, provided the processing is strictly necessary and all specified conditions are met [2]. These conditions include ensuring the bias cannot be effectively addressed using other data like synthetic or anonymised data [2]. Additionally, the data must be secured with strict controls and access limitations, subject to technical limitations on re-use, and deleted once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends [3][4][5]. This exception applies only when the bias is likely to affect health and safety, impact fundamental rights, or lead to prohibited discrimination [1]. The Act does not create an obligation to conduct such bias detection and correction [1].

No, predicting whether someone will commit a crime based solely on profiling is prohibited. Article 5 explicitly forbids the use of an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons to predict the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or assessing personality traits [1]. While Annex III lists certain law enforcement AI systems as high-risk, it specifically excludes systems that assess risk "not solely on the basis of the profiling of natural persons" [2].

No, the use of biometric categorisation systems that infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation is prohibited [1]. This prohibition specifically covers systems that categorise individuals based on their biometric data to deduce or infer these attributes [1]. While the Act prohibits such inferences generally, it does not cover labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets based on biometric data [1]. Additionally, AI systems intended for biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes are listed as high-risk systems [2].

Yes, an AI tool that screens and filters job applications is considered a high-risk AI system. According to Annex III, AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, specifically to analyse and filter job applications, are listed under the area of employment, workers' management, and access to self-employment [1]. These systems fall under the classification of high-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 6(2) [1].

Yes, an AI system intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score is a high-risk AI system [1]. However, this classification does not apply to AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud [1].

No, AI systems used solely for non-safety related aspects such as performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, or convenience do not qualify as safety components [1]. However, if the failure or malfunctioning of such an AI system would endanger health and safety, it would qualify as a safety component [2]. A safety component is defined as a component whose intended purpose is to prevent or mitigate risks to health and safety of persons or property [5].

Yes, AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the supply of water, gas, heating, or electricity are classified as high-risk [1]. However, such systems only qualify as safety components if their failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety [3]. AI systems used solely for non-safety related aspects like service efficiency or convenience do not qualify as safety components [2]. High-risk AI systems must also be resilient regarding errors and faults, potentially using technical redundancy solutions [4].

Yes, providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated [1]. However, this obligation does not apply if the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics [1]. Additionally, deployers of deep fake content must disclose that it has been artificially generated or manipulated, with exceptions for authorized criminal investigations or certain artistic and fictional works [3]. For text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, disclosure is required unless the content undergoes human review or editorial control [3]. Providers of such systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with these marking requirements by 2 December 2026 [2].

People must be given the information that they are interacting with an AI system at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure [2]. Similarly, deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate deep fake content must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated at the time of the first interaction or exposure [3]. This information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner [2].

Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must take the necessary steps to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026 [2].

A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 10^25 [1]. This threshold applies to the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 51 [1]. The Commission may also adopt delegated acts to amend these thresholds in light of evolving technological developments [1].

Yes, providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation [1]. This requirement applies to all providers of general-purpose AI models, and the documentation must contain specific information as set out in Annex XI [1][3]. The technical documentation must include details such as the model's architecture, inputs and outputs, and known or estimated energy consumption [3][4]. Providers must provide this documentation upon request to the AI Office and national competent authorities [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must perform model evaluation using standardised protocols and tools that reflect the state of the art, including adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks [1]. They are required to assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level stemming from the development, placing on the market, or use of these models [1]. Additionally, they must keep track of, document, and report serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office and national competent authorities without undue delay [1]. These providers must also ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure [1]. They may rely on codes of practice or European harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance with these obligations [4].
Providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must take the necessary steps to comply with the obligations laid down in the Regulation by 2 August 2027 [1].

The maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice is up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, the maximum fine for such non-compliance is up to EUR 1 500 000 [2]. These prohibitions apply to specific AI practices, such as the use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes [3] and the inference of emotions in workplace and education institutions [4].

A company can receive an administrative fine of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to national competent authorities [1]. This penalty applies to the supply of such information in reply to a request [1]. Additionally, for providers of general-purpose AI models, the Commission may impose fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, if they supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information pursuant to Article 91 [2]. The determination of the fine amount considers the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement, as well as commitments made in relevant codes of practice [2].

When deciding the amount of an administrative fine, authorities must consider all relevant circumstances of the specific situation. These factors include the size, annual turnover, and market share of the operator [4]. Authorities also consider whether administrative fines have already been applied to the same operator for the same infringement by other market surveillance authorities [3], or for other Union or national law infringements resulting from the same activity by other authorities [5]. Additionally, they take into account any financial benefits gained or losses avoided directly or indirectly from the infringement [1], as well as the degree of cooperation with national competent authorities to remedy the infringement [2].

The Commission may impose fines not exceeding 3 % of the provider's annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher [1]. The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review these decisions and may cancel, reduce, or increase the fine [2]. When fixing the amount, the Commission must consider the nature, gravity, and duration of the infringement while adhering to principles of proportionality and appropriateness [1]. The Commission shall also take into account commitments made under Article 93(3) or relevant codes of practice under Article 56 [1].

You can lodge a complaint with the AI Office if you suspect a provider or deployer of an AI system referred to in Article 75(1) is non-compliant [1]. Additionally, downstream providers have the right to lodge a complaint alleging an infringement of the Regulation against a provider of a general-purpose AI model [2]. The complaint must be duly reasoned and include specific details such as the point of contact of the provider, a description of the relevant facts, and the provisions of the Regulation concerned [2]. The AI Office may exercise its powers to investigate such complaints on its own initiative or following a complaint received pursuant to Article 85 [1].

Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, of at least six months [2]. Deployers of high-risk AI systems must also keep such logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months [1]. Both providers and deployers may be exempt from this requirement if applicable Union or national law, particularly Union law on the protection of personal data, provides otherwise [1][2]. Financial institutions acting as providers or deployers must maintain these logs as part of the documentation required under relevant Union financial services law [1][2].
